source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Galatas (in catenis)
Gal: Prolog
Τοῦ κηρύγματος εἰς τὰ ἔθνη δεχθέντος τινὲς τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς περιτομῆς ἐξιόντες
ἔπειθον τὰ ἔθνη ἰουδαΐζειν, καὶ πρώτη περὶ τούτου φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν
Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν μὴ ὑποκεῖσθαι νόμῳ, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ
εἰδωλοθύτου καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ πορνείας· οὕτω γὰρ ἔδοξε τῷ ἁγίῳ
πνεύματι. ἐκράτησε δὲ τὸ νόσημα τοῦτο τῶν Galατῶν συμφώνως ἰουδαΐζειν
βουληθέντων. ἐπείσθησαν δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν διαστρεφόντων λεγόντων, ὡς οἱ λοιποὶ
ἀπόστολοι οὐ κωλύουσι τοὺς βουλομένους τηρεῖν τὸν νόμον. 299 Gal 1,4 ∆είκνυσιν
ὅτι οὐ Μωϋσῆς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ τοῦ κόσμου οὐδέ τις τῶν προφητῶν ἄλλος. οὐ δεῖ
τοίνυν ἡττᾶσθαι τοῦ μὴ σώσαντος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀποθανόντος. Gal 1,6–7 Εἰς
ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἕτερον, φησίν· τὸ γὰρ ἡμέτερον εὐαγγέλιον καὶ τὸ
τῶν ἀποστόλων ἐκτὸς ὑμᾶς εἶναι βούλεται νόμου. Gal 1,8–10 Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί
δὲ καὶ ἡ μεῖς; ὅτε ἐκηρύττομεν, πνεύματος ἁγίου δυνάμει ἐκηρύξαμεν· τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα
τὸ ἅγιον οὐ μετανοεῖ. ἐὰν οὖν ἄλλα εἴπωμεν, κατελίπομεν τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. ἔστω
οὖν καὶ ὁ κῆρυξ ἀνάθεμα, ἀθετῶν τὸ κήρυγμα. Παρ' ὃ παρελάβετε. οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν
ἐγώ, φησίν, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐγὼ ἐκήρυξα, καὶ ὑμεῖς παρελάβετε. οὔτε
ἐγὼ μετανοῶ κηρύξας, καὶ ὑμεῖς τηρήσατε ὃ εἰλήφατε. Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ
τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος
οὐκ ἂν ἤμην. μέλλων αὐτοὺς ὑπομιμνήσκειν τοῦ ἰδίου εὐαγγελίου, προλαβὼν
ἀσφαλίζεται ἵνα μὴ νομίσωσιν ὅτι θεραπεύει ὑπαγόμενος· ἐπιπλήττει γὰρ νουθετῶν.
εἰπὼν δὲ εἰ ἔτι, ἐδήλωσεν ὅτι ἤρεσκε ποτὲ ἀνθρώποις. τίσι δὲ ἤρεσκεν; παρ' ὧν
ἔλαβεν ἐπιστολὰς τοὺς εἰς ∆αμασκὸν πιστοὺς κακῶσαι. εἰ οὖν, φησίν, ἤρεσκον ἔτι
τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις, οὐκ ἂν ἐπίστευσα τῷ Χριστῷ. Gal 1,13 Τίς χρεία τῆς ἐν τῷ Ἰουδαϊσμῷ
ἀναστροφῆς ἀλλ' ἵνα δείξῃ, ὅτι οὐ προλήψει δουλεύει ἀλλ' ἀληθείᾳ· οὐ γὰρ μισήσας
τὸν νόμον ὑπέδραμε τὴν χάριν–ἐξεδίκει γὰρ αὐτόν–ἀλλ' εὑρὼν τὸ τέλειον ἀπέστη
τοῦ νόμου. Νῦν δείκνυσιν ὅτι πλέον τι τῶν περὶ Πέτρον ἔχει· οὐ γὰρ ἐζήλωσαν
ἐκεῖνοι ὑπὲρ τοῦ Ἰουδαϊσμοῦ ἀπειθοῦντες τῷ Χριστιανισμῷ ὡς ἐγώ. 300 μὴ τοίνυν
οἰηθῇτε ὅτι μισήσας τὸν νόμον ἦλθον εἰς τὴν χάριν– ἐξεδίκουν γὰρ τὸν νόμον–ἀλλ'
εὗρον τὸ τέλειον, καὶ οὐκ ἐξισῶ τὸν νόμον τῇ τελείᾳ χάριτι. Gal 1,16 Οὐ διαβάλλων
δὲ τοὺς ἀποστόλους τοῦτό φησιν, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἐστοίχησα θνητῇ σαρκί. Gal 2,16 Εἰ
γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων, ἐκ δὲ πίστεως ὅπου τὸ τῆς
εὐκολίας καὶ τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης μέγα, πῶς οὐκ ἀναγκαῖόν φησιν ἐάσαντας νόμον
ἀρκεῖσθαι τῇ χάριτι; ἐξ ἔργων νόμου λέγει μὴ δικαιοῦσθαι, οὐκ ἐξ ἐντολῶν· ἡ γὰρ
ἐντολὴ δικαιοῖ ἀκουομένη, τὸ δὲ ἔργον ἦν τὸ δυσκατόρθωτον.
thought_title: The Galatian sickness and why only Christ saves
orientation: Severianus explains how some from the circumcision persuaded Gentile believers to live as Jews, and Paul answers by defending grace against law keeping.
pass_a_gloss: When the proclamation to the Gentiles had been received, some going out from the circumcision were persuading the Gentiles to live as Jews, and a first inquiry about this appears to have happened in Antioch, that the apostles wrote not to be subject to law, but to abstain from what is sacrificed to idols and blood and what is strangled and sexual immorality; for so it seemed good to the holy spirit. And this sickness prevailed over the Galatians, when they with one mind wanted to live as Jews. And they were persuaded by those who corrupt, who say that the remaining apostles do not hinder those who wish to keep the law. He shows that Moses did not die for the world nor did any other of the prophets. Therefore one must not be overcome by the one who did not save, but by the one who died for us. To another good news which is not another, he says; for our good news and that of the apostles wishes you to be outside law. Let him be an angel, and why also we? When we proclaimed, we proclaimed by power of holy spirit; and the holy spirit does not change its mind. If then we say other things, we have abandoned the things of the spirit. Let even the proclaimer be accursed, setting aside the proclamation. Contrary to what you received. I did not proclaim, he says, and you did not receive, but both I proclaimed and you received. Neither do I change my mind after proclaiming, and you keep what you have received. For now do I persuade men or God? Or do I seek to please men? If I still pleased men, I would not be a slave of Christ. Since he is about to remind them of his own good news, taking the lead beforehand he secures himself lest they think that he flatters as he submits; for rebuking he admonishes. And by saying if still, he made clear that he once pleased men. And whom did he please? Those from whom he received letters to harm the believers in Damascus. If then, he says, I still pleased the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ. What is the need of the conduct in Judaism except in order that he may show that he serves not by prejudice but by truth; for not because he hated the law did he run under grace, for he was avenging it, but because he found the perfect thing he stood away from the law. Now he shows that he has something greater than those around Peter; for those men did not show zeal for Judaism while disobeying Christianity as I did. Therefore do not suppose that because I hated the law I came to grace, for I was avenging the law, but I found the perfect thing, and I do not make the law equal to the perfect grace. And he says this not accusing the apostles, but that I did not follow mortal flesh. For if no one of those who bear toil is justified by works, but by faith, where the mark of ease and the greatness of righteousness is, how does he say it is not necessary, after leaving law, to be content with grace? He says not to be justified by works of law, not by commandments; for the commandment justifies when it is heard, but the work was the thing hard to accomplish.

pass_b_english: Once the preaching had been received among the Gentiles, some men coming from the circumcision began persuading the Gentiles to live as Jews, and the first dispute about this matter seems to have arisen in Antioch, for the apostles wrote that believers should not be subject to the law but should abstain from food offered to idols and from blood and from what is strangled and from sexual immorality, for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit.

This sickness took hold of the Galatians, since they joined together in wanting to live as Jews, and they were persuaded by men who distort the truth and claim that the other apostles do not stop anyone who wishes to keep the law.
Severianus says Paul shows that neither Moses died for the world nor any other of the prophets, so we must not be mastered by one who did not save us but by Him who died for us.
Paul says, “to another gospel, which is not another” (Galatians 1:6-7), for our gospel and the gospel of the apostles want you to be outside the law.

Severianus asks, granted an angel, why does Paul also say 'we'? Paul means: when we preached we preached by the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit does not change His mind, so if we say anything different we have abandoned the things of the Spirit, and therefore let the preacher who sets aside the preaching be accursed.

Paul says, “what you received” (Galatians 1:9), and Severianus explains his meaning: it is not that I preached and you did not receive, but I did preach and you did receive, and just as I do not regret having preached, so you must hold fast to what you received.

Paul asks, “Am I now persuading men or God, or am I seeking to please men, for if I still pleased men I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10), and Severianus says Paul is about to remind them of his own gospel, so he first secures his position so they will not think he flatters them by yielding, for he rebukes them while he exhorts them, and by saying “still” he revealed that he once pleased men, and whom did he please but those from whom he received letters to harm the believers in Damascus, so Paul says, if I still pleased the Jews I would not have believed in Christ.

Severianus asks why Paul mentions his former life in Judaism except to show that he serves not from prejudice but in truth, for it was not because he hated the law that he fled to grace, since he had even avenged the law, but because he found what is perfect he left the law behind, and now Paul shows that he has something more than those around Peter, for they never showed zeal for Judaism by opposing Christianity as he did, so Paul says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law, for I had avenged the law, but I found what is perfect, and I do not equate the law with perfect grace.
Severianus says Paul speaks not to slander the apostles but to declare that he did not follow mortal flesh.

Severianus says Paul argues that if no one of those who bear the toil is justified by works but one is justified by faith, where ease is found and the greatness of righteousness, then how is it not necessary to leave the law behind and be content with grace, for when Paul says no one can be justified by works of the law he means works, not commandments, since a commandment justifies when it is heard, whereas the work was what was hard to accomplish.

problems.why: The Greek implies 'is justified' from the previous clause; 'life comes' adds a claim not present in the source.
problems.fix: but one is justified by faith

problems.quote: it is not that I did not preach and you did not receive
problems.source_quote: οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν ἐγώ, φησίν, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε
problems.why: The Greek denies a split ('not that I preached while you did not receive'); adding 'did not' before 'preach' flips the first clause's meaning.
problems.fix: it is not that I preached and you did not receive
problems.ruling: Greek denies 'I preached, you didn't'; English denies 'I didn't preach,' flipping ἐκήρυξα.

problems.quote: so, Severianus says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law
problems.source_quote: μὴ τοίνυν οἰηθῇτε ὅτι μισήσας τὸν νόμον ἦλθον εἰς τὴν χάριν
problems.why: Attributing this first-person defense to Severianus confuses the speaker; it is Paul speaking in Severianus's paraphrase.
problems.fix: so Paul says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law
problems.ruling: Paul's ἦλθον/ἐξεδίκουν are paraphrased as Severianus's 'I,' misleading the speaker.

problems.quote: if no one of those who bear the toil is justified by works
problems.source_quote: Εἰ γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων
problems.why: The participle modifies 'works' (works that bring toil, contrasting with the ease of faith), not 'no one' as people bearing toil.
problems.fix: if no one is justified by works that bring toil
problems.ruling: τῶν πόνον φερόντων modifies ἔργων (toilsome works), not people bearing toil.

problems.quote: seems to have arisen in Antioch, where the apostles wrote
problems.source_quote: φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν
problems.why: Greek ὅτι means 'because' or 'for,' not 'where'; rendering it 'where' falsely places the apostles' writing in Antioch.
problems.fix: seems to have arisen in Antioch, for the apostles wrote
problems.ruling: ὅτι is 'because' or content 'that,' not locative 'where' for ἀπέγραψαν.

problems.quote: Severianus asks, let him be an angel, then why mention ourselves as well, for when we preached
problems.source_quote: Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡ μεῖς; ὅτε ἐκηρύττομεν
problems.why: Keeping 'ourselves' and 'when we preached' under 'Severianus asks' makes Severianus sound like the original preacher instead of Paul and the apostles.
problems.fix: Granted an angel, Severianus asks, why does Paul also say 'we'? Paul means: when we preached
problems.ruling: ἡμεῖς and ἐκηρύττομεν are Paul/apostles; 'Severianus asks…we preached' misattributes voice.

edits.new: but one is justified by faith

edits.old: it is not that I did not preach and you did not receive
edits.new: it is not that I preached and you did not receive

edits.old: so, Severianus says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law
edits.new: so Paul says, do not think I came to grace because I hated the law

edits.old: seems to have arisen in Antioch, where the apostles wrote
edits.new: seems to have arisen in Antioch, for the apostles wrote

edits.old: Severianus asks, let him be an angel, then why mention ourselves as well, for when we preached
edits.new: Severianus asks, granted an angel, why does Paul also say 'we'? Paul means: when we preached

fixed: addition life-comes fixed: replaced with 'but one is justified by faith' to supply δικαιοῦται implied by ἐκ δὲ πίστεως
negation did-not-preach fixed: removed extra 'did not' to match οὐκ ἐκήρυξα μὲν ἐγώ ... ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐλάβετε denying I-preached-while-you-did-not-receive
speaker Severianus-says do-not-think fixed: changed to 'so Paul says' because μὴ τοίνυν οἰηθῇτε ὅτι μισήσας ... ἦλθον continues Paul's first-person defense
no edit for bear-the-toil: English 'no one of those who bear the toil' correctly renders Εἰ γὰρ ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων as partitive οὐδεὶς τῶν + substantive participle
mistranslation where fixed: changed to 'for the apostles wrote' because ὅτι in φαίνεται ζήτησις γεγενημένη ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ, ὅτι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἔγραψαν cannot mean 'where'
speaker Severianus-asks angel fixed: separated question from Paul's 'we' because Ἔστω ἄγγελος, διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἡμεῖς; ὅτε ἐκηρύττομεν is Paul the preacher, not Severianus

refereed.quote: if no one of those who bear the toil is justified by works
refereed.source_quote: ἐξ ἔργων οὐδεὶς δικαιοῦται τῶν πόνον φερόντων
refereed.why: The neuter participle modifies 'works' ('works that bring toil'), not 'no one'; the English wrongly restricts 'no one' to people bearing toil.
refereed.fix: if no one is justified by works that bring toil
refereed.ruling: τῶν πόνον φερόντων qualifies burdensome ἔργων; English wrongly makes "no one" partitive, shifting Paul’s works-versus-faith point.
